meta.title: Mantine vs styled-components (2026): Which option should you choose?
meta.description: Compare Mantine and styled-components in 2026: component library vs CSS-in-JS styling. Learn differences in features, performance, theming, and which fits your React project.

verdict: Choose Mantine when you want a batteries-included React component library with accessible, themeable UI primitives, hooks, and a cohesive design system out of the box. Choose styled-components when you need a flexible CSS-in-JS styling layer for an existing or custom design system and prefer writing component-scoped styles yourself. Many teams combine a component library with a separate styling approach, so the choice often depends on how much prebuilt UI you want versus how much styling control you need.

comparison.toolA: Mantine is a full-featured React component library that ships hundreds of UI components, layout primitives, hooks, and a theming system, aiming to cover most application UI needs directly. Its styling utilities and components are designed to work together as a cohesive design system rather than as a single-purpose styling tool.
comparison.toolB: styled-components is a CSS-in-JS styling library, not a component library: it lets you write component-scoped CSS using tagged template literals and JavaScript expressions. It provides no prebuilt UI components, so you build your own components and design system on top of it.

comparison.toolA: Mantine provides a broad catalog of ready-to-use components such as buttons, inputs, modals, data tables, date pickers, notifications, and navigation elements, which can significantly reduce the amount of UI code a team writes. Component APIs, accessibility details, and styling are maintained as part of the library, though exact component coverage and props can change between major versions.
comparison.toolB: styled-components ships no UI components; every button, input, and dialog must be built or sourced elsewhere. This offers maximum design freedom but shifts the full burden of building, testing, and maintaining accessible components onto your team.

comparison.toolA: Mantine offers its own styling system built around CSS modules, theme tokens, and component props, and it supports customization through theme overrides, style props, and utility classes. It is flexible within its design system, but teams that want a pure JavaScript-driven styling model may find it more opinionated.
comparison.toolB: styled-components uses a dynamic CSS-in-JS model where styles are defined alongside components and can depend on props and theme values at runtime. This gives fine-grained control over conditional styling and component variants, at the cost of requiring your team to design and maintain the styling conventions.

comparison.toolA: Mantine includes a structured theme object covering colors, typography, spacing, radius, and component defaults, plus support for automatic color scheme handling and CSS variables. This makes it straightforward to establish a consistent look across an application without building theming infrastructure from scratch.
comparison.toolB: styled-components supports theming through a ThemeProvider context that any styled component can consume, and it works with design tokens you define yourself. It is powerful and unopinionated, but you are responsible for building the token structure, theme switching logic, and documentation.

comparison.toolA: Mantine's approach leans on CSS and CSS modules with theme-driven variables, which generally avoids per-render style serialization and can produce predictable styling performance. Actual performance depends on bundle configuration, tree-shaking, and which components you import, so results vary by project setup.
comparison.toolB: styled-components performs style generation at runtime, which can add overhead in large, frequently re-rendering component trees, and server-side rendering requires setting up style collection to avoid flash-of-unstyled-content issues. Modern versions have improved performance, but the runtime CSS-in-JS model remains a consideration for highly dynamic interfaces.

comparison.toolA: Mantine has a substantial surface area because of its many components and conventions, so teams need time to learn the component APIs and theming model. In exchange, documentation is extensive and many common UI problems are solved before you start writing code.
comparison.toolB: styled-components has a smaller conceptual surface: if you know CSS, tagged template literals and prop-based styles are quick to pick up. However, teams must still invest in designing components, accessibility patterns, and styling architecture themselves, which can offset the initial simplicity.

comparison.toolA: Mantine is actively developed with regular releases, and its integrated nature means upgrades may affect both components and styling conventions across an application. Adoption is broad in the React community, but teams should review migration notes between major versions before upgrading.
comparison.toolB: styled-components is a widely used, mature library with a large body of existing usage and community knowledge. Its runtime CSS-in-JS model has faced growing competition from zero-runtime and utility-first approaches, so teams should weigh long-term architectural direction alongside current stability.

faq.q: Which tool should I choose for a new React application?
faq.a: If you want to ship a polished interface quickly and avoid building common components from scratch, Mantine is usually the more productive starting point because it provides accessible UI components and a theming system together. If your project has a highly custom visual design and you prefer writing your own component-scoped CSS, styled-components gives you more direct styling control but requires you to build the component layer yourself.

faq.q: Can Mantine and styled-components be used together?
faq.a: In principle they can coexist in the same application, since styled-components generates its own class names while Mantine relies on its styling system and CSS modules. Teams sometimes use a component library for structure and a CSS-in-JS tool for bespoke pieces, but maintaining two styling paradigms can complicate theming, bundle size, and onboarding, so evaluate whether the added flexibility justifies the overhead.

faq.q: Does styled-components work with server-side rendering?
faq.a: Yes, styled-components supports server-side rendering, but it requires additional setup such as collecting generated styles during the render pass and injecting them into the HTML response. Without that configuration, users may see a flash of unstyled content, so teams using frameworks with SSR should follow the library's documented integration guidance and verify behavior for their framework version.

faq.q: Is Mantine a replacement for a styling library?
faq.a: Mantine includes its own styling and theming approach, so for many applications it can replace a separate styling library for the majority of UI work. However, it is not a drop-in substitute for every CSS-in-JS pattern, and teams with existing design systems may still need additional tooling or customization to match their brand and workflows.

faq.q: Which option is better for accessibility?
faq.a: Mantine components generally include accessibility considerations such as keyboard interaction and ARIA attributes as part of the library, which can reduce the effort needed to meet accessibility requirements, though you should still test your specific implementation. With styled-components, accessibility depends entirely on how you build your components, so your team must implement and audit semantics, focus management, and keyboard behavior directly.

faq.q: How do bundle size and performance compare?
faq.a: Mantine's CSS-based styling approach generally avoids runtime style generation, and bundle size depends heavily on which components you import and how your build handles tree-shaking. styled-components adds a runtime for generating styles and can incur more overhead in large, dynamic component trees, though actual impact varies with application structure and version, so measure your own build rather than relying on general claims.

faq.q: What are the main risks of choosing styled-components in 2026?
faq.a: The main risk is architectural: runtime CSS-in-JS has been losing ground to zero-runtime and utility-first styling approaches, and your team remains responsible for building all UI components and accessibility behavior. styled-components remains a mature, usable library, but teams should confirm it fits their framework support, performance budget, and long-term maintenance plans before committing.

faq.q: How hard is it to migrate between Mantine and styled-components?
faq.a: Migration effort depends on how deeply each tool is embedded in your codebase: moving from styled-components to Mantine involves replacing custom components with library equivalents and adapting theming, while moving from Mantine to styled-components requires rebuilding the entire component layer. Neither migration is mechanical, so plan for incremental adoption, thorough visual regression testing, and review of version-specific migration guides.
